persona.name: Deepak Joshi
persona.background: Deepak works irregular long hours and often skips meals when work is scarce. He has limited access to regular medical follow-up and presents only when symptoms become severe.

diagnoses.name: Myxedema Madness (severe hypothyroidism with neuropsychiatric manifestations)
diagnoses.description: Severe hypothyroidism presenting with hypothermia and neuropsychiatric manifestations such as confusion, disorientation, psychosis, delusions or hallucinations; depression is common.

diagnoses.name: Sick Euthyroid Syndrome/Nonthyroid Illness State (NTIS)
diagnoses.description: Changes in thyroid function tests during systemic illness, surgery, or fasting not caused by primary thyroid or pituitary dysfunction; commonly shows low T3 and treatment with thyroxine is not recommended.

diagnoses.name: Subclinical Hypothyroidism
diagnoses.description: Increased serum TSH with normal serum free T4; common in women and elderly and may progress to overt hypothyroidism.

diagnoses.name: Addison’s Disease (Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
diagnoses.description: Chronic adrenocortical insufficiency with fatigue and weight loss; cardinal features include hypotension and pigmentation; associated with autoimmune diseases.

diagnoses.name: Acute Adrenal Crisis/Addisonian Crisis
diagnoses.description: Acute presentation of primary adrenal failure with hypotension and acute circulatory failure with shock, dehydration, unexplained hypoglycemia and fever; biochemical abnormalities include hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

diagnoses.name: Cushing’s Syndrome
diagnoses.description: Features include central obesity, hypertension, proximal myopathy, purplish striae, bruising, glucose intolerance/diabetes, and neuropsychiatric symptoms; diagnosis requires confirmatory tests demonstrating inappropriate cortisol secretion.

diagnoses.name: Ectopic ACTH Secretion
diagnoses.description: Causes impaired glucose tolerance, hypokalemic alkalosis due to mineralocorticoid activity of cortisol, and skin pigmentation.

diagnoses.name: Primary Hyperparathyroidism
diagnoses.description: Often asymptomatic hypercalcemia; classical symptoms include 'moans, bones, stones, abdominal groans' with psychiatric manifestations, renal stones/polyuria and skeletal issues.

diagnoses.name: Subclinical Hyperthyroidism
diagnoses.description: Normal serum free T4 and T3 with subnormal TSH (<0.5 mU/L); may normalize or progress; cardiac effects include resting tachycardia and atrial fibrillation.

diagnoses.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
diagnoses.description: Gradual onset over months to years with polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, blurred vision, unexplained weakness or weight loss; may present with complications.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Myxedema madness** refers to severe **hypothyroidism** presenting with prominent **neuropsychiatric** symptoms such as delirium, psychosis, or cognitive slowing. **Cognitive slowing** - Marked slowing of thinking, speech, and responses due to low thyroid hormone states.
**Cold intolerance** - Feeling unusually cold from reduced basal metabolic rate and impaired thermogenesis.
**Weight gain** - Increased body weight from fluid retention and reduced metabolism, not rapid weight loss.
**Constipation** - Reduced gut motility causing infrequent stools and abdominal discomfort in hypothyroidism.
**Bradycardia** - Slow heart rate from decreased sympathetic tone and reduced myocardial contractility.
**Nonpitting edema (myxedema)** - Glycosaminoglycan deposition causing doughy swelling, especially face and extremities.

This patient instead has a shock-like presentation with **severe hypotension**, **tachycardia**, dehydration, vomiting, and electrolyte disturbances (**hyponatremia** with **hyperkalemia**) that strongly indicate **primary adrenal insufficiency** with **acute adrenal crisis**. The rapid deterioration over two weeks with near-syncope and volume depletion is far more consistent with adrenal crisis than decompensated hypothyroidism. Additionally, the lab pattern and hemodynamics align with **mineralocorticoid deficiency** rather than hypothyroid physiology.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Sick Euthyroid Syndrome (NTIS)** is an adaptive alteration in thyroid hormone levels during acute or chronic systemic illness without intrinsic thyroid gland disease. **Fatigue/weakness** - Nonspecific constitutional symptoms driven by the primary illness, not thyroid failure itself.
**Hypothermia or low metabolic state** - May be seen in severe illness, but not a defining presenting complaint.
**Altered mental status** - Can occur due to critical illness; not specific to NTIS and varies widely.
**Weight loss** - Often due to catabolism/poor intake from illness; not typically rapid endocrine-driven wasting.

Clinically, patients present with features of the precipitating illness rather than a primary thyroid syndrome, and the diagnosis is supported by thyroid function tests (low **T3**, variable **T4**, low/normal **TSH**). In this case, the dominant findings are **profound hypotension**, **dehydration**, **vomiting**, **hyponatremia**, and **hyperkalemia**, which strongly indicate **acute adrenal crisis** rather than a thyroid hormone adaptation pattern.

**Electrolytes** - NTIS has no characteristic **hyponatremia with hyperkalemia** pattern; **acute adrenal crisis** classically causes **hyponatremia, hyperkalemia** due to aldosterone deficiency.
**Primary pathophysiology** - NTIS is an adaptive thyroid hormone change during illness; **acute adrenal crisis** is life-threatening **cortisol (± aldosterone) deficiency**.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Addison’s disease** is chronic **primary adrenal insufficiency** due to progressive destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, causing deficient **cortisol** and often **aldosterone**. **Weight loss** - Progressive loss of appetite and catabolism over months due to chronic adrenal hormone deficiency.
**Nausea/vomiting** - Recurrent gastrointestinal upset seen in chronic adrenal insufficiency, usually less abrupt than crisis.
**Postural dizziness** - Orthostatic symptoms from chronic **aldosterone deficiency** causing salt wasting and low volume.
**Hyperpigmentation** - Diffuse darkening of skin/mucosa from elevated **ACTH** in primary adrenal failure.

However, the presentation is dominated by severe shock physiology (BP 80/40, tachycardia, near-syncope) evolving over days to weeks, which is more consistent with **acute adrenal crisis** rather than stable chronic Addison’s disease. **Dizziness/near-syncope** - Indicates severe **hypotension** from volume depletion and impaired catecholamine responsiveness.
**Hypotension (80/40 mm Hg)** - Hallmark of adrenal crisis; due to low cortisol and aldosterone causing shock.

**Hyperkalemia (K+ ~5.9 mmol/L)** - From mineralocorticoid deficiency causing impaired renal potassium excretion.
**Eosinophilia** - Cortisol normally suppresses eosinophils; elevation supports adrenal insufficiency.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Cushing’s syndrome** is a state of chronic **glucocorticoid excess** due to exogenous steroids or endogenous cortisol overproduction. **Dorsocervical fat pad** - Posterior neck/upper back fat accumulation producing a “buffalo hump.”
**Proximal muscle weakness** - Difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs due to steroid myopathy.
**Purple striae** - Wide violaceous stretch marks on abdomen/thighs from dermal collagen breakdown.
**Easy bruising** - Fragile skin and capillaries causing ecchymoses with minimal trauma.
**Hypertension** - Sustained elevated blood pressure from cortisol’s mineralocorticoid effects and vascular sensitivity.
**Hyperglycemia** - Elevated glucose or diabetes due to increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance.
**Osteoporosis** - Bone loss and fracture risk from inhibited osteoblast function and calcium imbalance.
**Recurrent infections** - Increased susceptibility due to cortisol-mediated immunosuppression.

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about vomiting and diarrhea (dehydration/salt deprivation).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Textbook states adrenal crisis occurs with dehydration due to salt deprivation, vomiting, or diarrhea; these are common precipitants and explain acute deterioration.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: History of vomiting and/or diarrhea with dehydration preceding shock/weakness suggests adrenal crisis trigger.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “...exposed to the stress of infection, trauma, surgery, or dehydration due to salt deprivation, vomiting, or diarrhea.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about recent infection or unexplained fever.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Infection is a major stressor precipitating crisis; fever can be part of the presentation (“unexplained fever”).
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Recent infectious illness and/or fever supports a precipitating stress for adrenal crisis.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “...exposed to the stress of infection...” and “...abdominal tenderness ‘acute abdomen’ and unexplained fever.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about recent trauma or surgery.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Trauma and surgery are listed stressors that can precipitate acute adrenal crisis in Addison’s disease.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Recent trauma/surgery preceding collapse supports adrenal crisis precipitated by stress.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “...exposed to the stress of infection, trauma, surgery...”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about nonspecific symptoms: weakness, fatigue, lethargy, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion or coma.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: These are the textbook’s nonspecific symptoms of acute adrenal crisis and help recognize the syndrome.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Cluster of these symptoms (especially vomiting/abdominal pain/confusion) supports adrenal crisis presentation.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Nonspecific symptoms: Weakness, fatigue, lethargy, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion or coma.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about features suggesting long-standing adrenal insufficiency: weight loss and prior episodes of acute adrenal crisis after stress/slow recovery from illness.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Crisis in long-standing adrenal insufficiency may show chronic features; prior crisis history is a cardinal clue to Addison’s disease.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Weight loss and/or previous crisis following stress (or slow recovery from illness) supports underlying Addison’s disease with acute crisis.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Crisis in patients with long-standing adrenal insufficiency... may show hyperpigmentation... weight loss...” and “Cardinal features of Addison’s disease: Hypotension, pigmentation and previous history of acute adrenal crisis following stress, or slow recovery from illness.”

keyExaminations.action: Assess for shock and hypotension (hemodynamic status).
keyExaminations.reasoning: Shock out of proportion to severity of illness and hypotension are major manifestations of adrenal crisis and acute primary adrenal failure.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Hypotension/shock disproportionate to illness severity supports adrenal crisis.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Major manifestations: Shock (out of proportion to severity of illness)” and “Acute: Hypotension and acute circulatory failure with shock...”

keyExaminations.reasoning: Abdominal tenderness and ‘acute abdomen’ are listed clinical features of adrenal crisis.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Abdominal tenderness consistent with ‘acute abdomen’ supports adrenal crisis presentation.

keyExaminations.action: Inspect skin and mucous membranes for hyperpigmentation (including palms/oral mucosa).
keyExaminations.reasoning: In long-standing primary adrenal insufficiency, crisis may show hyperpigmentation due to chronic ACTH hypersecretion; pigmentation is nearly always present in primary (not secondary) adrenal insufficiency.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Hyperpigmentation of exposed/pressure areas, palmar creases, mucous membranes supports primary adrenal insufficiency background.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “...may show hyperpigmentation (due to chronic ACTH hypersecretion)...” and “Skin pigmentation is nearly always present in primary adrenal insufficiency (but not in secondary).”

keyInvestigations.action: Order serum electrolytes and glucose immediately.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Textbook directs withdrawing blood for serum electrolytes and glucose; typical abnormalities include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and others.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia (± hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, azotemia) support adrenal crisis.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Withdraw blood for serum electrolytes, glucose...” and “Laboratory Findings: Hyponatremia, Hyperkalemia... Hypoglycemia.”

keyInvestigations.action: Send plasma cortisol and ACTH (do not wait for results).
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Textbook explicitly recommends routine plasma cortisol and ACTH sampling in suspected crisis and not delaying treatment for results.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Inappropriately low cortisol with elevated ACTH supports adrenal insufficiency (primary AI suggested by elevated ACTH).
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “...routine plasma cortisol and ACTH. Do not wait for results.” and “Plasma ACTH level: Elevated in adrenal insufficiency.”

keyInvestigations.action: If not a known case of adrenal insufficiency, perform a short ACTH stimulation test.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Textbook states to do short ACTH stimulation test when the patient is not a known case; failure of cortisol rise confirms adrenal insufficiency.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Failure of rise in plasma cortisol after 0.25 mg synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin) supports adrenal insufficiency.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “In case patient is not a known case of AI, do short ACTH stimulation test.” and “ACTH stimulation test: There is failure of rise in plasma cortisol level... 0.25 mg... cosyntropin.”

keyInvestigations.action: Measure early morning (6 am) cortisol level (if evaluating adrenal insufficiency outside immediate crisis sampling).
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Textbook provides diagnostic cutoffs for early morning cortisol to suggest or exclude adrenal insufficiency.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Cortisol <3 µg/dL suggests adrenal insufficiency; >11 µg/dL excludes AI (random cortisol 20 µg/dL in ill patient is reassuring).
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Early morning (6 am) cortisol level... Levels <3 µg/dL is suggestive... Levels >11 µg/dL exclude AI... Random cortisol in ill patient 20 µg/dL reassuring.”

keyInvestigations.action: If tuberculous adrenalitis is suspected, order chest radiograph and consider abdominal plain radiograph/CT/MRI for adrenal calcification.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Textbook notes imaging findings for tuberculous adrenalitis (pulmonary TB evidence and adrenal calcification on imaging).
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Chest radiograph evidence of pulmonary tuberculosis and/or adrenal calcification on abdominal radiograph/CT/MRI supports tuberculous adrenalitis as cause.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Radiograph: In patients with tuberculous adrenalitis: Chest radiograph may show evidences of pulmonary tuberculosis and plain radiograph of abdomen, CT scan, and MRI scan may show calcification in the adrenal gland.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Look for pigmentation (nearly always present in primary but not secondary) and interpret ACTH (elevated in adrenal insufficiency; pigmentation reflects chronic ACTH excess).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Skin pigmentation is nearly always present in primary adrenal insufficiency (but not in secondary).” and “Plasma ACTH level: Elevated in adrenal insufficiency.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal hemorrhage following meningococcemia)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Consider when adrenal crisis follows meningococcemia; look for cutaneous petechiae/purpuric lesions with abrupt profound prostration and shock.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “...Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage... following meningococcemia (Waterhouse‒Friderichsen syndrome).” and “...fulminant meningococcal septicemia... produces cutaneous petechiae... vasomotor collapse, and shock... Abrupt in onset and profound prostration...”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Primary adrenal failure presenting as acute vs chronic Addison’s disease
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Differentiate acute crisis features (hypotension/shock, dehydration, acute abdomen, unexplained hypoglycemia/fever) from chronic features (postural hypotension, salt craving, pigmentation, weight loss).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Primary adrenal failure may present. Acute: Hypotension... shock... dehydration, an ‘acute abdomen’, unexplained hypoglycemia, and unexplained fever... Chronic: ...postural hypotension and salt craving.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Suspect acute adrenal crisis in a patient with shock (out of proportion to illness) plus nonspecific symptoms (weakness, fatigue, lethargy, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion/coma) and/or abdominal tenderness with unexplained fever, especially after stressors such as infection, trauma, surgery, or dehydration from vomiting/diarrhea/salt deprivation. Examine for hypotension/shock, abdominal tenderness, and (if long-standing primary adrenal insufficiency) hyperpigmentation and weight loss. Immediately establish IV access and withdraw blood for serum electrolytes and glucose plus plasma cortisol and ACTH (do not wait for results). Typical labs include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia (± hypercalcemia, azotemia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia). If the patient is not a known case of adrenal insufficiency, perform a short ACTH stimulation test to confirm adrenal insufficiency, then determine the type of adrenal insufficiency; consider imaging for tuberculous adrenalitis when suspected (chest radiograph and abdominal radiograph/CT/MRI for adrenal calcification).
